title: The energy in sunlight spent millennia escaping the Sun
body: Energy released by fusion in the Sun’s core doesn’t fly straight out. In the dense interior, light is absorbed and re-emitted in random directions over and over, a zigzag “random walk” that takes the energy somewhere between 10,000 and 170,000 years to reach the surface, depending on the estimate. After that long struggle, the final dash from the Sun’s surface to your skin takes only about 8 minutes and 19 seconds.

slides.question: Once it leaves the Sun’s surface, how many seconds does light take to reach Earth?
slides.explanation: About 8 minutes and 19 seconds, around 500 s. Getting from the core to the surface takes far longer: a random walk estimated at anywhere from 10,000 to 170,000 years.

slides.alt: Animation: the Sun opens into a labelled cutaway of its core, radiative zone and convection zone. Zoomed in, light zigzags outward in a random walk; a gauge shows the 10,000 to 170,000 year estimate; light then crosses to Earth as a clock runs to 8:19.

slides.prompt: Watch the photon zigzag until it escapes the model Sun. How many steps does it need to get 20 steps from the centre?
slides.takeaway: About 400: a random walk needs roughly the square of the distance in steps. Across the real Sun, that squaring turns a dash light could make in two seconds into many thousands of years.

slides.heading: A long way out, a short way here
